summary:
Wyoming's facilities law is the most immediate exposure for a trans visitor. House Bill 72, the "Protecting privacy in public spaces act," was signed by Governor Mark Gordon on 3 March 2025 after passing the House 52-8 on 7 February 2025 and the Senate 25-6, and took effect 1 July 2025. It defines male and female by biological sex and requires public facilities to reserve multi-occupancy restrooms, changing areas and sleeping quarters exclusively for males or exclusively for females, prohibiting entry into a facility that does not match biological sex. Accommodations are permitted only where they do not involve access to opposite-sex multi-occupancy facilities. The law creates a private cause of action for a person who encounters an opposite-sex person in a sex-designated restroom or changing area where the facility permitted it or failed to prohibit it, and for a person required by a correctional or educational facility to share sleeping quarters with the opposite sex.

Schools carry a parallel mandate. Senate File 62, "Sex-designated facilities and public schools," also signed 3 March 2025, requires public school children from pre-kindergarten up, including charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth, and requires districts to provide a "reasonable accommodation" to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth.

Wyoming's equality-map entry documents these facility bans signed in March 2025 among the state-level bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities matching their gender identity.

State identity documents are changeable but with conditions. Changing the gender marker on a Wyoming birth certificate requires sex reassignment surgery and a court order stating sex has been changed, submitted to Vital Statistics Services with a letter requesting the change, a photocopy of current ID, a certified copy of the court order, and a doctor letter confirming surgery was performed. Correction of the gender marker on a Wyoming driver's license or state ID requires a completed Gender Designation Change Request Form signed by the applicant and a physician, therapist or counselor, psychiatric social worker or other medical or social service provider confirming gender identity.

Nondiscrimination protection is thin. Wyoming state statutes do not address discrimination based on gender identity in public accommodations, housing, employment, or credit/lending. As of 12 October 2026 the state's gender-identity policy score stands at -9/25 with an overall score of -6.5/47, rated Negative, the sole noted protection being federal recourse for employment discrimination based on gender identity available nationwide since the June 2020 Bostock ruling through the EEOC and federal courts. The cities of Jackson, Casper and Laramie have local ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations.

Wyoming has no state hate crime law. The federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of 2009, which covers bias-motivated violence based on gender identity, applies in its place.

Trans athletes are barred from school sports. A bill passed by both houses in March 2023 (SF133, approved 1 March 2023) bans transgender students from playing sports consistent with their gender identity; it became law without the governor's signature or veto and took effect 1 July 2023.

Gender-affirming care for minors is prohibited. A bill passed by both houses in March 2024 explicitly bans sex reassignment surgery and gender-affirming care on children; the governor signed it to take effect 1 July 2024.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment by Erin Reed, drawing on five years of daily legislative tracking, lists Wyoming among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults; the assessment was republished 27 August 2026 by a regional LGBTQ outlet and also records federal policies creating legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.
tangentialFactors:
Same-sex marriage has been recognized in Wyoming since 21 October 2014, after state officials declined to appeal the 17 October federal decision in Guzzo v. Mead finding the ban unconstitutional; that decision replaced a statutory ban in place since 1977 and made more explicit in 2003, under which legal relationships of same-sex couples had been recognized only for divorce. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since Wyoming decriminalized consensual sodomy in February 1977, with common-law liability for anal intercourse abrogated in 1982; the age of consent for all consensual sexual activity is 17.

Married same-sex couples are permitted to adopt, and state law recognizes the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status. State law does not authorize or prohibit gestational surrogacy contracts, leaving review case-by-case; an August 2021 law explicitly legalizing surrogacy contracts uses the terms mother and father rather than parent or parents, which excludes single people and same-sex couples.

A 2013 domestic partnership bill to provide immediate-family rights was approved 7-2 in House committee on 28 January but rejected 24-35 by the full House on 30 January. State statutes do not address discrimination based on sexual orientation; prohibitory bills were rejected by the House on 31 January 2011 and by the Senate 15-13 on 31 January 2013, and bill SF 115, approved 24-6 by the Senate and 6-2 in House committee in February 2015, was rejected 26-33 by the House on 24 February 2015. Cheyenne and Gillette prohibit city employment discrimination on sexual orientation only.

A state obscenity-material law affecting certain LGBT books was enforced in October 2021 when a Gillette librarian was charged by the district attorney and sheriff's office.

Wyoming's lack of a state hate crime statute followed the hot debate after the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard near Laramie; the federal 2009 Act covers sexual orientation as well as gender identity.
localsOnly:
Residents face the full scope of House Bill 72 and Senate File 62 in daily life: sex-designated multi-occupancy restrooms, changing areas and sleeping quarters in all public facilities, and school facilities assigned by sex at birth from pre-kindergarten onward, with only limited reasonable accommodations available.

State identity documents are changeable through defined procedures. A birth certificate gender-marker change requires sex reassignment surgery plus a court order, filed with Vital Statistics Services alongside a request letter, photocopy of current ID, certified court order, and doctor's letter confirming surgery. A driver's license or state ID gender-marker change requires a Gender Designation Change Request Form signed by the applicant and a qualifying medical or social service provider confirming gender identity.

Employment discrimination based on gender identity has no state statutory prohibition; recourse runs through the EEOC and federal courts under Bostock. Residents of Jackson, Casper and Laramie are additionally covered by local ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Cheyenne and Gillette cover sexual orientation in city employment only.

Wyoming has no state hate crime law; gender-identity bias-motivated violence is prosecutable only under the federal 2009 Act.

Transgender students are barred from school sports teams consistent with their gender identity under SF133, effective 1 July 2023. Gender-affirming care and sex reassignment surgery for children are banned under the March 2024 law effective 1 July 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not document any Wyoming-specific incident of violence against a trans person, any enforcement action under House Bill 72 or Senate File 62, or any arrest or private cause of action filed under the law's civil-remedy provisions; whether the cause of action has been used is unresolved here.

Whether the facility statutes have been challenged in court, and their current litigation status, is not sourced.

The inventory does not state whether Wyoming has adopted any rule restricting which facilities trans visitors may use in state parks, federal land, or tribal lands within Wyoming, including the Wind River Reservation; tribal-nation-specific rules are not sourced.

Wyoming's position in the July 2026 do-not-travel state count is not specified in this inventory; only its listing among the worst states for anti-trans legislation is documented.

Whether any Wyoming state agency has issued guidance implementing federal passport or visa marker rules at state-identity-document level is not sourced.
